title: Temperament
description: The biologically based, early‑appearing, relatively stable foundation of personality. Temperament is the “raw material” that life experience sculpts into full personality.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: The biologically based, early‑appearing, relatively stable foundation of personality. Temperament is the “raw material” that life experience sculpts into full personality.

sections.title: Core Characteristics
content: Emotional reactivity: how strongly and quickly a person responds to stimuli.
Activity level: overall energy and movement.
Sociability: tendency to seek others.
Adaptability: ease of adjusting to change.
Persistence/attention span: ability to stay focused despite obstacles.

sections.title: Behavioral Patterns
content: High reactivity: cries easily, startles, intense emotional expressions from infancy.
High activity: always on the move, fidgeting, difficulty sitting still.
High sociability: seeks out others, smiles at strangers.
High adaptability: goes with the flow, adjusts to new routines quickly.
High persistence: practices a skill for hours, won’t give up on a puzzle.

sections.title: Communication Style
content: Reactive: dramatic, emotional language.
Low reactive: calm, subdued tone.
Persistent: asks many questions, argues points.

sections.title: Strengths
content: High reactivity: passion, empathy (if channeled).
High activity: productivity, physical skill.
High adaptability: resilience in changing environments.

sections.title: Weaknesses
content: High reactivity: emotional overwhelm, drama.
High activity: restlessness, impulsivity.
Low adaptability: distress over minor changes.

sections.title: Decision-Making Style
content: High persistence: thorough but slow.
High impulsivity (low persistence): quick, sometimes reckless.
High reactivity: emotion‑driven.

sections.title: Relationship Patterns
sections.content: Temperamental mismatch causes friction. A low‑reactivity partner may misunderstand a high‑reactivity partner’s tears.

sections.title: Workplace Behavior
content: High‑activity people hate boring, static jobs.
Low‑adaptability people struggle with frequent re‑orgs.

sections.title: Leadership Style
content: Reactive leaders are passionate but can create tension.
Persistent leaders are dogged but can micromanage.

sections.title: Stress Response
sections.content: Inborn. Some infants cry for hours; some are soothed easily. This forms the base of adult stress patterns.

sections.title: How to Identify It
content: Ask about childhood: “What kind of baby were you?”
Observe how they react to unexpected changes and sensory input (noise, crowds).

sections.title: Common Misconceptions
content: Temperament is not destiny. Environment and effort can shape it.
“Difficult temperament” doesn’t mean bad; it means challenging to parent, but can be a strength in adulthood.

sections.title: Real-World Scenario
sections.content: Two siblings grow up in the same household. One was a calm baby, slept through the night, smiled at everyone. The other screamed for hours, hated new people. As adults, the first is laid‑back; the second is anxious and intense. Their temperaments steered them down different paths despite the same parenting.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: You arrived with a blueprint. Life renovated the house, but the original foundation still shows.
